# Modern mode

@difference Extension: one comment at the top of a program, `;#pragma modern`, turns on the newer behaviour of BlitzLLVM, and the original reads it as a comment.

BlitzLLVM builds programs the way the original does, quirks included, so that old programs keep working. A few of those quirks have a better alternative that changes what a program does, so they are off unless the program asks for them. Modern mode asks for all of them at once:

```blitzbasic
;#pragma modern
Type Player
	Field lives% = 3
End Type
p.Player = New Player
Print p\lives ; 3 in modern mode, 0 in the original.
```

The original Blitz3D and BlitzPlus see a comment and build the program as always, so one file works in both.

## The features

| Pragma | Option of `blitzcc` | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `modern` | `--modern` | All of the features below. |
| `sane-evaluation-order` | `--sane-evaluation-order` | Arguments, operators, array indices and stores are evaluated from left to right, see [Language Quirks](Language-Quirks#left-to-right). |
| `field-defaults` | `--field-defaults` | `New` sets fields to their default values (`Field lives% = 3`), see [Language Quirks](Language-Quirks#default-values-of-fields). |

`modern` always means every feature of the BlitzLLVM that builds the program, so a newer BlitzLLVM can add more. A program that has to stay the same lists the features it wants instead of `modern`. `no-` in front of a name turns a feature off again, and the last pragma for a feature wins:

```blitzbasic
;#pragma modern no-field-defaults
```

Several names can be on one line, separated by spaces or commas, or on several `;#pragma` lines. Names don't care about upper or lower case.

## Where it goes

These pragmas belong in the comments at the top of the **main file**, the one given to `blitzcc`, before its first statement. Empty lines and other comments may come before them. After the first statement they do nothing and warn `pragma-misplaced`.

The main file decides for the whole program, `Include`d files too: a `Type` from an included file is used by the code of the main file, so both have to agree on how it works. An included file can say what it was written for with the same pragmas. If that doesn't match the program, it warns `pragma-mismatch`, and the file is still built the way the main file says:

```text
lib.bb:1:10: warning: 'lib.bb' was written for a program that evaluates from left to right, but this one evaluates in the order of the original. [-Wpragma-mismatch]
```

The pragmas of the main file win over the options of `blitzcc`, and the options win over the default of the original. A name that this BlitzLLVM doesn't know warns `pragma-unknown` and does nothing, so a program for a newer BlitzLLVM still builds.

## Warnings

The same `;#pragma` line can change the warnings from where it is on, for example `;#pragma Wno-implicit-variable` or `;#pragma warning(push)`. Unlike the features, these can be anywhere and carry through `Include` like in C, see [Warnings](Warnings#in-the-program).

## In the editor

The Visual Studio Code extension shows the warnings above while typing.
